messages.author: 99feee15920ab812
messages.subject: Badgers
parts:
Dear Distance users,

I am working on a project that needs to estimate the density of European
Badgers (Meles meles). There are two questions that have arisen from
this.

1. In our study area the badgerÕs setts are invariably in woodland, but
the majority of their foraging is done on surrounding fields. Using
spotlights on open land is very effective so there is no problem there.
The woodland, however does pose significant problems. Observing badgers
in woodland is extremely rare and a spotlight is almost a hindrance due
to the shadows it throws.

The question is: Can we estimate the population for the whole area by
just sampling the open land? We have an idea but I thought it would be
prudent to check with the experts first.

What we do know: a) the total area of the site, b) the area of the
woodland, and c) the area of open land. We can also assume that the each
individual will forage on the open land most nights. Is it right assume
that the population estimate derived from just sampling the open land,
will be an accurate estimate of the population for the total area? i.e.
a higher density estimate but less area (just open land) as opposed to a
lower density and a bigger area(open land plus woodland). What would the
limitations of this approach be?

2. Badgers live in extended family groups and maintain fairly strict
territories. Obviously when they first emerge from the sett in the
evening they are concentrated in a small area. How should the sampling
account for this. Our approach is to wait until two hours or so after
the emergence to allow them to spread as homogeneously as possible. Is
there any other considerations to be aware of? Is there any problems
with the territorial nature of these animals?

I hope this mail is clear, and IÕll look forward to any suggestions.

Regards,

Tim Hounsome.

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Badgers
parts:
> > 1. In our study area the badgerÕs setts are invariably in woodland, but
> > the majority of their foraging is done on surrounding fields. Using
> > spotlights on open land is very effective so there is no problem there.
> > The woodland, however does pose significant problems. Observing badgers
> > in woodland is extremely rare and a spotlight is almost a hindrance due
> > to the shadows it throws.
> >
> > The question is: Can we estimate the population for the whole area by
> > just sampling the open land? We have an idea but I thought it would be
> > prudent to check with the experts first.
> >
> > What we do know: a) the total area of the site, b) the area of the
> > woodland, and c) the area of open land. We can also assume that the each
> > individual will forage on the open land most nights. Is it right assume
> > that the population estimate derived from just sampling the open land,
> > will be an accurate estimate of the population for the total area? i.e.
> > a higher density estimate but less area (just open land) as opposed to a
> > lower density and a bigger area(open land plus woodland). What would the
> > limitations of this approach be?

This approach works provided all badgers are in open country at the time
you survey. If not, then you estimate only that part of the population
that is in the open area. It doesn't matter if you include or exclude the
woodland area in your calculation. If you include it, you get an average
density across woodland and open land; as the woodland density is assumed
to be zero (no badgers seen there), that will give you a lower density
than if you exclude it - but then you multiply by a larger overall area,
which compensates. If, as seems more realistic, some badgers occur in
woodland, you ideally need supplementary studies to estimate the
proportion in woodland at the time of the surveys -
e.g. radio-tagging. Failing that, you can adjust the area surveyed around
points to take account of areas that are not visible, but you then have to
assume that density in woodland is the same as elsewhere, so that approach
isn't worth pursuing.

> > 2. Badgers live in extended family groups and maintain fairly strict
> > territories. Obviously when they first emerge from the sett in the
> > evening they are concentrated in a small area. How should the sampling
> > account for this. Our approach is to wait until two hours or so after
> > the emergence to allow them to spread as homogeneously as possible. Is
> > there any other considerations to be aware of? Is there any problems
> > with the territorial nature of these animals?

That seems a good strategy. Clustering doesn't matter, except it reduces
precision a little, so giving them time to disperse will improve precision
... and possibly reduce the numbers that remain in woodland.

Steve

messages.author: 3c3dc0b6f44a7cbf
messages.subject: Re: Badgers
parts:
Tim,

I would suggest that it would be much simpler to use some sort of cue
counting method using dung pits, latrines and even better - setts themselves
(you could stratify by the number of holes or the size of the mound etc).

Without knowing exactly what you are doing, it is hard to give any more
advice. I would suggest reviewing your aims and establishing whether
Distance is the right method to use. I apologise in advance if this is
telling you what you already know and there are good reasons why you would
not want to use these methods (not knowing more about the aims of the
project), but.....

Probably better to identify all known setts and feeding tracks etc (there
are standard methods for doing this and it is possible to identify different
clans by bait marking etc - quite intensive study but much simpler to get an
overview). I would then suggest that you concentrate on each main sett /
annex, identifying if they are active or not and then perhaps counting
individuals as they emerge - again assuming that you are trying to get as
close to an exact population as possible and you are doing a study over a
relatively small area (I know a project that has done this over about 6
square kilometres). If it is part of large scale monitoring, perhaps you
could consider sampling.

It's just a hunch, but I reckon that Distance is not really practical for
this project. Even with a lot of effort, I would doubt that your confidence
limits would be nearly good enough to be of practical use. So much is known
about the life history and behaviour of Badgers that you can design a much
better and more accurate short-term study using other published methods.

Having said that, I would be very interested to know if Distance data on
dung pits and latrines can be correlated with Badger populations / number of
clans. Has anyone done this sort of experiment?

I don't know if this will help, but here are some references:

Cresswell, P., Harris, S. & Jefferies, D. J. (1990) The history,
distribution, status and habitat requirements of the badger in Britain.
JNCC, Peterborough.
Harris, S., Jefferies, D., Cheeseman, C. & Booty, C. (1994) Problems with
Badgers? RSPCA, Horsham.

Regards,

Simon Mustoe.
